en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Robes 10.
The Training Rule on Kings:
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a high official who was a supporter of the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta sent a messenger with a robe-fund for the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta, saying:
"Having purchased a robe with this robe-fund, clothe the noble Upananda in a robe.
Then that messenger approached the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta; having approached, he said this to the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta:
“Venerable sir, this robe-fund has been brought for the sake of the venerable Upananda.
May the venerable one accept the robe-fund.
When this was said, the venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta said this to that messenger:
“Friends, we do not accept cloth-money; rather, we accept robes at the proper time when they are allowable.
When this was said, that messenger said to the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan-son:
“Does the Venerable have anyone who acts as his agent?”
Now at that time, a certain lay follower came to the monastery on some business.
Then the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son said this to that messenger:
"This lay follower, friend, is a service-provider for the monks."
Then that messenger, having persuaded the lay follower, approached the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son; having approached him, he said this to the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son:
"Venerable sir, the one whom the Venerable designated as a service-provider has been informed by me.
Let the Venerable approach at the proper time; he will clothe you with the robe-cloth."
Now at that time, the chief minister sent a messenger to the venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta, saying:
"May the noble one use that robe; we wish for the noble one to use that robe.
But the venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta said nothing to that lay follower.
A second time, that great minister sent a messenger to the venerable Upananda, the son of the Sakyans, saying:
"May the noble one use that robe; we wish for the noble one to use that robe.
A second time, the venerable Upananda, the son of the Sakyans, said nothing to that lay follower.
A third time, that chief minister sent a messenger to the venerable Upananda, the son of the Sakyans, saying:
"May the noble one use that robe; we wish for the noble one to use that robe.
Now at that time, it was the market day of the town.
And a formal agreement had been made by the merchants: "Whoever arrives last shall be fined fifty [pieces].
Then the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan went to that lay follower; having approached him, he said to that lay follower, "I have need of a robe, friend."
“Venerable sir, wait until tomorrow; today is the market day for the town.
An agreement has been made by the townspeople that whoever arrives late shall be fined fifty [pieces].
“Give me my robe this very day, friend,” he said, and he felt about his waistband.
Then that lay follower, being pressured by the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan-son, went after having had a robe purchased for the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan-son.
People said this to that lay follower:
"Why have you come late, noble sir? You have lost fifty [pieces of money]."
Then that lay follower explained the matter to those people.
The people complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"These recluses, sons of the Sakyan, are full of great desires and lack contentment."
"It is not easy even to perform a service for these people.
How indeed could the Venerable Upananda, when told by a lay follower,
'Venerable sir, please wait until tomorrow,' fail to come?"
The bhikkhus heard those people grumbling, complaining, and criticizing.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... [and so forth]... they grumbled, complained, and criticized:
"How can the venerable Upananda the Sakyan son allow himself to be provided with [robes] by a lay follower?"
“‘Venerable sir, please wait until tomorrow,’ he will not wait when told this.
Then those monks, having rebuked the venerable Upananda the Sakyan son in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One.
… “Is it true, Upananda, that you [acted thus] with a lay follower?”
“Venerable sir, when he was told, ‘Wait today, bhante,’ he did not wait.
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him … [as before] …
"How indeed, foolish man, could you not come when you were told by a lay follower, 'Venerable sir, please wait until tomorrow'?
"This, foolish man, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so forth]."
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:
“If a king, a royal official, a brahmin, or a householder, on behalf of a certain monk, should send a messenger with a gift for purchasing robes, saying:
‘Having purchased a robe with this gift for purchasing robes, clothe such-and-such a monk with a robe,’ [then that monk should inform the messenger:]”
If that messenger, having approached that bhikkhu, should speak thus:
“Venerable sir, this robe-fund has been brought for the venerable one; may the venerable one accept the robe-fund,” then that bhikkhu should say this to the messenger:
‘Friends, we do not accept cloth-money; however, we do accept robe-cloth that is appropriate and given at the right time.
If that messenger should say to that bhikkhu, ‘But does the venerable one have anyone who acts as his agent?’”
“Monks, a monk who needs robes should point out a steward— either a monastery attendant or a lay follower—
saying, ‘This person, friends, is the steward for the monks. If that messenger, having informed that steward, approaches the monk and speaks thus:”
“Venerable sir, that person whom the venerable one designated as a service-provider has been informed by me: ‘Let the venerable one approach at the proper time; he will clothe you with a robe.
Monks, a monk who needs a robe should approach the service-provider and, after two or three times, should remind him and prompt him, saying:
‘Friend, I have need of a robe.’”
If, by urging and reminding him two or three times, he should cause that robe to be produced, that is good.
If he should not cause it to be produced, he should stand silently for that purpose four, five, or at most six times.
If, while standing silently for that purpose four, five, or at most six times, he should cause that robe to be produced, that is good.
If, by striving further than that, he should obtain that robe-cloth, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If he does not obtain it, he should either go there himself or send a messenger to the place where the robe-fund was brought, saying:
"Venerable sirs, the robe-fund which you sent for the sake of a certain monk has not served any purpose for that monk."
“Venerable sirs, apply yourselves to your own [task]; let not your own [task] perish”—this is the proper conduct in that regard.
“Having designated a bhikkhu,” however, means:
"For the sake of a bhikkhu" means: having made a bhikkhu the object, desiring to clothe a bhikkhu.
"A king" refers to anyone who exercises sovereignty.
One who is called a "royal retainer" (rājabhogga) is anyone whose food and wages are provided by the king.
One who is called a "brahmin" (brāhmaṇa)...
By birth one is a brahmin.
One called a householder—
excluding the king, those dependent on the king, and the brahmin— is the rest, who are called householders.
"An acquisition for robes" means gold, silver, pearls, or gems.
"By this acquisition for robes."
"By one who has presented [it].
"Having bartered" means having exchanged.
"Cover it" means "give it.
If that messenger, having approached that bhikkhu, should speak thus:
“Venerable sir, this robe-fund has been brought for the sake of the venerable one. May the venerable one accept the robe-fund.
That monk should say to that messenger:
“Friends, we do not accept robe-funds. We accept robes themselves, at the proper time and if they are allowable.”
If that messenger should say to that bhikkhu,
"Does the venerable one have anyone to perform services for him? then,
monks, a bhikkhu who needs robes should point out a service-provider, whether a monastery attendant or a lay follower.
“This, friend, is the attendant for the monks.
One should not say to him, “Give this to him,” or “He will set it aside,” or “He will exchange it,” or “He will have it bartered for.
If that messenger, having persuaded the attendant, approaches that monk and speaks thus:

“Venerable sir, the person whom the Venerable One pointed out as a service-provider has been informed by me. Let the Venerable One approach him at the proper time; he will clothe him with the robe-cloth.
Monks, a monk who needs robe-cloth should approach the service-provider and, after two or three times, remind and prompt him, saying:
“Friend, I have need of robe-cloth.”
One should not say: "Give me a robe; bring me a robe; exchange a robe for me; have a robe purchased for me.
This may be said a second time and a third time.
If he succeeds in obtaining it, that is well.
If he does not succeed, he should go there and stand silently, designating [the meal] for himself.
He must not sit on a seat. He must not accept any food.
One should not preach the Dhamma.
When asked, "For what reason have you come?", one should say, "Know for yourself, friend.
If he sits on a seat, or accepts material gifts, or preaches the Dhamma, he breaks his standing.
A second time he should stand;
a third time he should stand.
Having exhorted him four times, he should stand four times.
Having urged [the donor] five times, he should stand [waiting] twice.
Having urged six times, he should not stand.
If, by striving beyond that, he succeeds in obtaining that robe-cloth, [he commits an offense].
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the act of using it.
By the mere acquisition [of the item], it becomes subject to relinquishment (nissaggiya).
It must be relinquished to the Saṅgha, or to a group (gaṇa), or to an individual (puggala).
And thus, monks, it should be relinquished:
“… ‘Venerable sir, this robe-cloth of mine, which was produced after being pressed three times by urging and six times by standing, is to be relinquished.’”
“I relinquish this to the Saṅgha. … “One should give it” … “They should give it” … [and so on].
"I give it to the Venerable One.
If he should not succeed [in obtaining the robe], then one must either go there in person or send a messenger with the robe-fund that was brought for him, saying:
"Venerable sirs, the robe-fund which you sent for the sake of that bhikkhu has served no purpose for that bhikkhu."
“Let the venerable ones apply themselves to their own [welfare]; let not your own [welfare] perish.
This is the proper conduct therein;
this is the accordance with the Dhamma therein.

If, after more than three admonitions and more than six standings, one procures [the robe] while perceiving it as being more than that, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If, after more than three admonitions and more than six standings, one procures [the robe] while being in doubt as to whether it is more than that, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If, after more than three admonitions and more than six standings, one procures [the robe] while perceiving it as being less than that, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If one has admonished fewer than three times and stood [to give the formal act] fewer than six times, yet perceives it as more, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one has admonished fewer than three times and stood fewer than six times, yet is uncertain, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one has admonished fewer than three times and stood fewer than six times, and perceives it as fewer, there is no offense.
There is no offense:
if one has admonished three times and stood [waiting] six times;
or if one has admonished fewer than three times and stood fewer than six times.
One gives without being urged;
the owners give after having been urged;
[the case of] one who is insane.
"For one who is a first-time offender.
The tenth training rule concerning kings is concluded.
The first chapter on the Kathina is finished.
Its summary verse:
The suspension of the kaṭhina, three [cases],
washing, and receiving.
Three with strangers,
and for both [monks and nuns] by messenger.
